body:
State Disaster Management Authority

Every state has a State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) under section 14 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005. In a state such as Gujarat, the SDMA is chaired by the Chief Minister.

The State Authority develops and coordinates state-level disaster-management policy and planning. Under the 2025 amendments, it coordinates the preparation and approves the State Disaster Management Plan. It also approves District Plans and Urban Plans prepared by the competent authorities.

State-level responsibilities include identifying risks, promoting preparedness, coordinating departments, setting relief standards that cannot be lower than NDMA's minimum standards and maintaining a state disaster database.

State Executive Committee

The State Executive Committee (SEC) is chaired by the Chief Secretary. It assists the SDMA and coordinates and monitors the implementation of national and state disaster-management plans.

The 2025 amendment also added the Director General of Police of the state as an ex-officio member of the SEC. This is an institutional membership provision, not a transfer of the Chief Secretary's chairmanship.

The distinction resembles that at the national level: the SDMA has the principal state policy and planning role, while the SEC has important coordination and implementation responsibilities.

District Disaster Management Authority

The District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) is the main district-level planning, coordinating and implementing body. Under section 25, it is chaired by the District Collector, District Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner, according to the designation used in the district.

The DDMA also includes an elected local-government representative as co-chairperson. Where a Zila Parishad exists, its Chairperson is the co-chairperson under section 25(3). In the Sixth Schedule tribal areas, the Chief Executive Member of the autonomous district council is the ex-officio co-chairperson.

Other statutory members include the district's Superintendent of Police, Chief Medical Officer and the Chief Executive Officer of the DDMA. The 2025 amendment allows the state to appoint up to 2 additional members from district-level officers, disaster-management experts or civil-society organisations.

The DDMA identifies district hazards and vulnerable locations, prepares the District Disaster Management Plan, coordinates departments, promotes public awareness, maintains preparedness and supervises arrangements for warnings, relief and response.

Local authorities: action closest to the community

Local authorities include Panchayati Raj institutions and urban local bodies. They are important because they understand local settlements, roads, public facilities and the people who may require assistance.

Under section 41 of the national Act, local authorities must, subject to DDMA directions, undertake responsibilities including:

  • Training their officers and employees for disaster management.
  • Maintaining relevant resources so that they are available when needed.
  • Ensuring that construction projects within their jurisdiction follow applicable disaster-prevention and mitigation standards.
  • Carrying out relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction activities in accordance with the State and District Plans.
  • Preparing their own disaster-management plans, as expressly added to section 41 by the 2025 amendment.

The Gram Sabha provides a forum for villagers to participate in local decision-making and hold the Gram Panchayat accountable. The Gram Panchayat can contribute to local preparedness through community awareness, identification of vulnerable residents, maintenance of local facilities and coordination with the DDMA. The Gram Sabha and Gram Panchayat are not the same institution.

Urban Disaster Management Authorities

Section 41A, inserted in 2025, allows a state government to establish a separate Urban Disaster Management Authority for its state capital and cities having a Municipal Corporation, excluding the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Chandigarh.

If constituted, the Urban Authority is chaired by the Municipal Commissioner, with the District Collector as vice-chairperson. It prepares an Urban Disaster Management Plan for approval by the SDMA and coordinates the implementation of that plan.

The provision is enabling: a state government may constitute an Urban Disaster Management Authority by notification. The mere existence of a Municipal Corporation does not prove that such an authority has been established.

Gujarat's institutional development

The earthquake of 26 January 2001 was a turning point in Gujarat's disaster-management arrangements. It demonstrated the need for organised recovery, safer reconstruction and long-term preparedness.

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) was initially established and registered as a society on 8 February 2001 to coordinate the earthquake recovery programme and support disaster preparedness and mitigation.

Gujarat subsequently enacted the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003. The Bill was passed in the Legislative Assembly on 28 March 2003, and the Act came into force on 13 May 2003. The statutory GSDMA began functioning under that Act with effect from 1 September 2003. Its headquarters are at Gandhinagar.

These dates represent different events: the creation of the original society, the commencement of the state legislation and the establishment of the statutory authority. Gujarat's state legislation preceded the national Disaster Management Act, 2005.

The Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management (GIDM), established on 26 January 2004, supports disaster-management education, training and capacity-building for officials and other stakeholders. GIDM is a training institution; GSDMA is the state disaster-management authority.

Gujarat's example shows how post-disaster reconstruction can become the starting point for a broader system of preparedness, mitigation, training and risk-informed development.

Prelims focus

  • SDMA: chaired by the Chief Minister.
  • SEC: chaired by the Chief Secretary.
  • DDMA: chaired by the District Collector, District Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner.
  • Urban Authority, if constituted: Municipal Commissioner as Chairperson and District Collector as Vice-Chairperson.
  • GSDMA: established as a society on 8 February 2001; statutory authority from 1 September 2003.
  • Trap: The Gujarat Act took effect on 13 May 2003, not on the date the original GSDMA society was created.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, sections 14, 18, 20, 25, 30, 31 and 41; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, amendments to sections 18, 20, 25 and 41 and insertion of section 41A; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, Constitution and History, and About Us, consulted 2 November 2026; GSDMA, Establishment of Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Social and Political Life I, Class 6, chapter 5, Panchayati Raj, printed pp. 43–48.]

body:
Why disaster-management plans are needed

A disaster-management plan identifies likely hazards, vulnerable people and assets, available resources, responsible institutions and arrangements for prevention, preparedness, response and recovery. Without these agreed arrangements, departments may duplicate work, overlook vulnerable groups or delay essential assistance.

India's statutory framework provides for plans at several levels. A national plan establishes broad responsibilities and priorities, while state, district, urban and local plans translate them into arrangements suited to their respective areas.

Who prepares and approves the plans?

The 2025 amendment is particularly important because it revised planning responsibilities and review intervals. The following table describes the legal position under the amended national Act.

PlanPreparation and approvalReview or update requirement
National PlanNDMA coordinates preparation and approval in consultation with governments and other stakeholders.Review once every 3 years; update at least once every 5 years.
State PlanSDMA coordinates preparation and approves the plan.Review once every 3 years; update at least once every 5 years.
District PlanDDMA prepares it after consultation with local authorities; SDMA approves it.Review and update at least once every 2 years, or earlier as necessary.
Urban PlanUrban Authority prepares it, if that authority has been constituted; SDMA approves it.No separate interval specified in section 41A.
Local-authority planLocal authority prepares its plan under DDMA supervision.Must be reviewed and updated regularly and be consistent with applicable district-level planning requirements.

Central and state government departments must also prepare plans covering their own responsibilities. For example, a department responsible for essential public services must identify how it will reduce risks, maintain preparedness and perform its assigned functions during an emergency.

Do not apply an outdated annual-review rule to the National, State or District Plans. The 2025 amendment introduced the review and update intervals stated above. Also distinguish review, which examines a plan, from update, which revises its contents.

Disaster funds: response and mitigation

Disaster-management activities require money for immediate assistance and for reducing future losses. The national Act provides separate categories of response funds and mitigation funds.

Response funding supports the financial needs of disaster management according to applicable statutory provisions and government guidelines. Mitigation funding addresses measures intended to reduce disaster risk and likely future damage.

National-level funds

  • National Disaster Response Fund: provided for under section 46. The 2025 amendment broadens its statutory purpose to meeting different aspects of disaster management. Its application follows guidelines laid down by the Central Government in consultation with NDMA.
  • National Disaster Mitigation Fund: provided for under section 47 for disaster-mitigation needs. Its application also follows Central Government guidelines framed in consultation with NDMA.

Under section 8B, the High Level Committee deals with the financial assistance to states envisaged under section 46 and approves assistance for mitigation needs under section 47.

State- and district-level funds

Section 48 provides for 4 funds to be established by state governments:

  • State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF): made available to the State Executive Committee.
  • District Disaster Response Fund: made available to the District Disaster Management Authority.
  • State Disaster Mitigation Fund: made available to the State Disaster Management Authority.
  • District Disaster Mitigation Fund: made available to the District Disaster Management Authority.

The 2025 amendment specifies the arrangements for making these funds available to the relevant authorities. The actual use of money is governed by the applicable statutory provisions and financial guidelines; the existence of a fund does not imply that every reported loss is automatically reimbursable.

Do not confuse a disaster response force with a response fund

The abbreviation NDRF is used for 2 very different things:

  • National Disaster Response Force: specialist personnel and capabilities for disaster response, under section 44.
  • National Disaster Response Fund: a financial arrangement under section 46.

Similarly, SDRF can refer to a State Disaster Response Fund or, in a different context, a State Disaster Response Force. The 2025 amendment expressly permits state governments to constitute a State Disaster Response Force under section 44A. In a question, the surrounding words personnel, rescue, deployment or funds, assistance, finance help identify which meaning is intended.

How coordination works during a disaster

Consider severe flooding affecting several villages in a Gujarat district. Local authorities can help identify affected households, communicate warnings and arrange temporary assistance. The DDMA coordinates district departments, essential supplies, shelters and response arrangements. The SEC coordinates relevant state departments, while the SDMA provides state-level policy and planning direction.

If the situation requires assistance beyond available state resources, national institutions can support the state through specialist response, coordination and financial arrangements. The primary responsibility of the state government and the supporting role of the Central Government are complementary.

Connecting the whole subject

Disaster management can be understood through 3 related questions. First, what creates risk? Hazards interact with exposure, vulnerability and capacity. Second, what should be done? Prevention, mitigation and preparedness reduce losses; response and relief protect people; recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction restore and improve community life. Third, who is responsible? National, state, district, urban and local institutions share defined planning, coordination, operational and financial responsibilities.

The most important principle is that disaster management should reduce future risk as well as address present emergencies. Better planning, public participation, strong institutions and safer recovery can interrupt the process by which hazards become disasters.

Prelims focus

  • National and State Plans: review every 3 years; update at least once every 5 years.
  • District Plan: review and update at least once every 2 years, or earlier as necessary.
  • District Plan approval: SDMA; preparation: DDMA.
  • Section 46: National Disaster Response Fund; section 47: National Disaster Mitigation Fund.
  • Section 48: state and district response and mitigation funds.
  • Trap: National Disaster Response Force and National Disaster Response Fund share the abbreviation NDRF but have different functions.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, sections 11, 18, 23, 31, 32, 37, 40, 41 and 44–49; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, amendments to sections 11, 18, 23, 31, 41, 46, 47 and 48 and insertion of sections 8B and 44A; Ministry of Home Affairs, Press Information Bureau, parliamentary reply on disaster-management responsibilities and the 2025 amendment, 22 July 2025. Statutory provisions and commencement status checked for the content cutoff of 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Risk foundations connect to management before and after a disaster, supported by governance and funds, with reduced losses feeding back into future risk.
